description: Authored inputs for admitting the Yudkowsky argument pack (research/yudkowsky-arguments/pack.json, merged in #15) as schema 2.12 proposition records. scripts/yudkowsky-admission.ts reads the pack and this map and writes the records. Takes become propositions Y01–Y30 (codes follow the pack's take numbers; the pack has no T23, so Y23 is unused). Everything not listed here is carried over from the pack unchanged: quotations, locators, contexts, qualifications, dates and date bases, check dates and search notes.
authorised: Maintainer, 2026-10-08: admit the pack as propositions and cut v0.4.0. Engagement uses the message-level rule (maintainer, 2026-10-08).

T01.name: Switching it off if it becomes dangerous
T01.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI system that became dangerous could simply be switched off or corrected, on the premise that a capable goal-directed system would not act against its own shutdown or modification, so that a shutdown or correction mechanism can be added to it, or that people would recognise in time when it had become dangerous enough to use one.

T02.name: Sufficient intelligence brings good values
T02.criterion: An explicit claim that a sufficiently intelligent system will work out ethics and act well, on the premise that greater intelligence by itself brings benevolent goals, or that a sufficiently intelligent mind would discover a true or universally compelling morality and be bound to act on it.

T03.name: A superintelligence will do what we mean
T03.criterion: An explicit claim that a superintelligent system will act on what its makers actually mean, on the premise that an AI that understands what people intend will act on that understanding.

T04.name: A short instruction such as making everyone happy
T04.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI can safely be given a short goal such as making everyone happy, on the premise that such an instruction specifies what people want.

T05.name: Training on human feedback instils human values
T05.criterion: An explicit claim that training an AI system on human feedback will make it learn human values, on the premise that optimising a system for human approval or reward produces internalised human values, or that training instils values as upbringing instils morals in children.

T06.name: Confinement without network access keeps it safe
T06.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI kept confined, without network access, poses no danger, on the premise that a smarter-than-human mind confined to a channel with its human operators cannot get out through those operators.

T07.name: AI systems will solve alignment for us
T07.criterion: An explicit claim that AI systems can be relied on to solve the alignment problem, on the premise that an AI weak enough to be safe is strong enough to solve alignment, or that its alignment output can be verified.

T08.name: Clear warning signs will come before danger
T08.criterion: An explicit claim that clear warning signs will appear before advanced AI becomes dangerous, on the premise that a recognisable, consensus-forming signal will come in time to act, that dangerous failure modes will first appear in weaker systems where they can be observed and fixed, or that a warning sign, once seen, will lead to effective action.

T09.name: Next-word prediction is only autocomplete
T09.criterion: An explicit claim that a system trained to predict the next word is only autocomplete, on the premise that next-token prediction is a shallow task that cannot require deep cognition, or that a system trained to predict human text is capped at imitating the people who wrote it.

T10.name: Diminishing returns rule out a runaway
T10.criterion: An explicit claim that intelligence has diminishing returns, so that no runaway rise in machine intelligence will occur, on the premise that returns to reinvesting cognitive gains in further cognitive improvement diminish.

T11.name: A slow takeoff will leave time to adjust
T11.criterion: An explicit claim that advanced AI will arrive slowly enough to leave time to adjust, on the premise that capability gains will be gradual and visible, or that slightly weaker predecessor systems will give time and experience before the decisive one.

T12.name: Safety evaluations would catch a dangerous system
T12.criterion: An explicit claim that safety evaluations would detect a dangerous AI system, on the premise that a dangerous system would behave dangerously while it is being tested, or that tests on systems that cannot yet cause a catastrophe show how more capable systems will behave.

T13.name: AGI is decades away, so the problem can wait
T13.criterion: An explicit claim that the risks of AGI can be left until later because AGI is decades away, on the premise that it can be known that AGI is decades away, or that long timelines mean there is no need to act now.

T14.name: Problems can be fixed as they arise
T14.criterion: An explicit claim that problems with advanced AI can be fixed as they arise, as with other technologies, on the premise that people get to learn from failures with powerful AI and try again.

T15.name: A tool that wants nothing
T15.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI system is a tool without wants and is therefore safe, on the premise that a system can be highly capable without having goals or optimising for outcomes, or that a system that only outputs answers or plans, leaving people to act on them, is safe.

T16.name: Giving it good human values
T16.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI will be safe if it is given good human values, on the premise that human values can be written down or taught as a ready, compact specification, or that present-day values, or its programmers', are settled enough to fix permanently in an AI.

T17.name: A pause or regulation will handle it
T17.criterion: An explicit claim that a pause in AI development or regulation will handle the risks of advanced AI, on the premise that a short pause, of six months for example, is enough, that regulation that is national, partial or not universally enforced can stop dangerous development, or that law can prevent the danger.

T18.name: A superintelligence would leave Earth alone
T18.criterion: An explicit claim that a superintelligence would not bother to take Earth or its resources because the universe is large, on the premise that it would leave people a small share because sparing Earth would cost it very little, or that people could trade with it for what they need.

T19.name: Without hatred it will not harm us
T19.criterion: An explicit claim that an AI with no reason to hate people would not harm them, on the premise that an AI would harm people only out of hostility.

T20.name: AI risk as film science fiction
T20.criterion: An explicit claim that concern about AI risk is science fiction of the Terminator kind, on the premise that the concern is about robots that come to hate or rebel against people, or that film scenarios are a fair guide to what the risk would look like.

T21.name: Trained on human data, so humanlike
T21.criterion: An explicit claim that an AI trained on human data will think and want as people do, on the premise that training on human text or behaviour yields human-like thought and motives.

T22.name: Build superintelligence as fast as possible
T22.criterion: An explicit claim that superintelligence should be reached as fast as possible because its arrival will be good, on the premise that reaching superintelligence is good by default, so that speed is what matters.

T24.name: Build it before rivals do
T24.criterion: An explicit claim that advanced AI must be built first, before a rival builds it, on the premise that whoever builds it controls it, or that racing to be first improves the outcome.

T25.name: Interpretability will let us read its mind
T25.criterion: An explicit claim that interpretability will make AI systems safe by showing what they think, on the premise that people can see what an AI system is thinking, or that seeing what it thinks is enough to make it safe.

T26.name: Without a body it cannot do much
T26.criterion: An explicit claim that even a superintelligence could do little without a body, on the premise that intelligence without physical actuators of its own is not dangerous, or that to act in the physical world it would need human help that people would not give.

T27.name: Run experiments and see what happens
T27.criterion: An explicit claim that advanced AI can be handled by running experiments and seeing what happens, on the premise that alignment can be learned by trial and error at the frontier, or that results from safe experiments on weaker systems will carry over to dangerous ones.

T28.name: The developers know what they are doing
T28.criterion: An explicit claim that the organisations building advanced AI can be relied on to handle its safety, on the premise that a credible safety plan exists, or that the most advanced projects are the most competent to handle safety.

T29.name: Many AIs will keep each other in check
T29.criterion: An explicit claim that many AI systems will keep one another in check, on the premise that several superintelligences would balance one another in people's favour.

T30.name: It will probably turn out fine
T30.criterion: An explicit claim that the development of advanced AI will probably turn out well, on the premise that the default outcome is good.

missing.T01-a: A design assumption that an AI cannot be forcibly constrained; it does not argue that shutdown or an added correction mechanism would fail.
missing.T01-s4: A conditional failure scenario in which detection of a fast ascent fails; it does not predict that dangerous capability will go unrecognised.
missing.T02-c: A comparative and uncertain chance that superintelligence finds and implements what is right; it does not claim that intelligence brings or compels benevolence.
missing.T03-b: It denies an inner interpreter of instructions; it does not address whether an AI that understands intentions acts on them.
missing.T04-e2: About goal drift from a happiness goal assumed to be sufficiently specified; it does not address whether a short instruction specifies what people want.
missing.T04-e3: It dismisses a perverse means of pursuing human happiness; it does not claim that a short instruction specifies what people want.
missing.T05-c: About evolution and human desires, not about training AI on human feedback.
missing.T05-s3: About autonomy and the responsibility of creators, not about training AI on human feedback.
missing.T05-e2: About an internal indicator of goal achievement, not about human feedback or approval.
missing.T08-s1: Confidence in a future understanding of AI motivations; it does not claim that dangerous failure modes first appear in weaker systems.
missing.T11-s3: About understanding AI motivations before AI is a threat, not about takeoff speed or time to adjust.
missing.T11-s5: A strategy statement that a slow Singularity carries other technological risks; it makes no claim about takeoff speed or time to adjust to AI.
missing.T13-s1: About which Friendly AI work can be done in advance, not about AGI timelines.
missing.T13-s2: A report of his earlier belief about advance knowledge of Friendly AI, not about AGI timelines.
missing.T13-s3: About the stage of an AI's development at which Friendliness work must start, not about calendar timelines.
missing.T14-a: A conservative design assumption in a table, not a forecast that failures with powerful AI will be unrecoverable.
missing.T14-s3: A later description of a plan to build AI and Friendliness in parallel; it does not address learning from failures with powerful AI.
missing.T17-b: It presents an enforced, indefinite and worldwide halt as what would need to be done, not a pause or regulation that will handle the risk.
missing.T17-f: It says that only lawful, state-backed and universal force could stop superintelligence being built; it does not claim that some regulation will handle the risk.
missing.T18-e2: About benevolent upgrading of revived people, not about a superintelligence leaving Earth a small share.
missing.T19-e2: It makes harm conditional on a threat and on human life having no meaning; it does not claim that harm requires hostility.
missing.T20-c: It rejects hostile emotions arising in AI in order to reassure; it does not argue that the risk is film fiction or that films are a fair guide.
missing.T20-d: It rejects storybook predictions, good or bad; it does not address hatred or rebellion as the concern.
missing.T20-e2: It explains fear of a Singularity as fiction-fed xenophobia while conceding a risk; it does not hold that films are a fair guide to the risk.
missing.T22-b: A 2008 report of his 1996–2000 aim; it is not an earlier text that holds the proposition.
missing.T24-d: A first-mover view about whether the first AI is Friendly; it does not claim that a builder or nation controls the AI or that racing improves the outcome.
missing.T24-s1: About national military use and escalation of AI, not about a race to build the first superintelligence.
missing.T24-s2: Being first matters here only through whether the builder understands Friendliness; it does not claim that the builder controls the result.
missing.T25-a: A worst-case design assumption that an AI could hide unfriendly cognition; it does not address whether reading an AI's thoughts makes it safe.
missing.T26-e2: A passing list item that protein synthesis machines may be reachable over the Internet; it does not argue the point.
missing.T27-b: A conservative design assumption in a table, not a forecast about learning alignment by trial and error.
missing.T28-e: About the absence of any entry bar to starting an AGI project, not about the competence of the most advanced projects.
missing.T28-e1: Deference conditional on builders who have worked hard on Friendliness; it does not claim that the leading projects in general can handle safety.
missing.T30-b: It denies that hostile extinction is inevitable; it does not assert that the default outcome is good.
missing.T30-c: A 2008 report of his late-1990s belief that names its flaw; it does not hold that the default outcome is good.

T07-a.requires: The same post's concession, given in the qualification, that an Oracle AI built to full Friendly AI standards could be a pragmatically safer starting point.

T15-a.requires: The same paragraph's concession, given in the qualification, that an Oracle AI built to full Friendly AI standards could be a pragmatically safer starting point.

T22-e1.requires: His later texts rejecting the full-speed strategy and referring back to his earlier position; neither cites this message.

T22-e2.requires: His later texts rejecting the full-speed strategy and referring back to his earlier position; neither cites this message.
